answer.rationale: With the primary contract expiring in 14 days and the line already at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, any action that introduces onboarding or qualification risk (switch_primary_vendor) is dangerous despite memory_c2's cost-cut appeal, especially since that record is a single-year, unverified data point. Memory_c4 shows that benchmarking-driven renegotiation at renewal has previously recovered real margin and improved payment terms without disrupting the existing, stable integration (reinforced by memory_c1's stability record and memory_c6's volume-pricing gains from longer commitments). Given the finance mandate for an 18% cut and the tight timeline, negotiating harder with the incumbent—potentially locking a multi-year term for better unit economics—directly addresses cost pressure while preserving delivery continuity. I verified memory_c4 and memory_c2 to confirm the negotiation outcome details and to check whether the low-cost vendor switch had any hidden delivery risk not captured in the summary, since these two memories most directly conflict on the best path to cost reduction. Second-sourcing (memory_c3) remains valuable for risk diversification but is a separate decision that can wait for the next review cycle since only one action fits this cycle's capacity.
